clue.text: Mobile stolen nearby – might this get people talking?

indicators.note: something mobile moves about, so the letters that follow are free to change places

explanation.surface: A phone has been pinched close by; will that set the neighbours gossiping?
explanation.walkthrough: The BLARNEY STONE, at Blarney Castle in Ireland, is said to give whoever kisses it the gift of the gab.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend says kissing the stone grants eloquence, so it is the thing that might get people chattering persuasively.

clue.text: Marsh bird seen in freezing cold November

blocks.note: N is November in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A wading bird spotted on a raw winter day.
explanation.definitionFit: The bittern is a heron-like bird of reed beds and marshes, famous for its booming call.

clue.text: Navy officer and rising US city lawyer touring border

indicators.note: to tour is to go round, so the lawyer's letters travel around the border
in a down entry, rising means the whole chain is read from the bottom up

explanation.surface: A naval man and a lawyer from an up-and-coming American city tour the frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising' applies to the whole of city, lawyer and border, not just the city. DA is the American District Attorney, a public prosecutor.
explanation.definitionFit: An admiral is a senior commissioned officer of a navy, commanding a fleet.

clue.text: Amateur in good shape for charity

blocks.note: an amateur is not a professional

explanation.surface: A weekend athlete keeps in trim to raise money for a good cause.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonprofit organisation exists for a charitable or public purpose rather than to make money.

clue.text: Long, spun-out story entertains European

indicators.note: a host entertains a guest inside their home, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: a yarn is a long rambling tale, and yarn is also spun

explanation.surface: A drawn-out tale keeps a continental visitor amused for ages.
explanation.definitionFit: To long for something is to yearn for it: both verbs mean to desire wistfully.

clue.text: All this is absurd, pretty implausible

indicators.note: something absurd makes no sense as it stands, so the letters must be put into a sensible order

explanation.surface: A sceptic dismissing a whole story as nonsense and hard to believe.
explanation.walkthrough: A tall story is one hard to believe, so tall means implausible and the -ish ending supplies 'pretty'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tall can mean exaggerated or unlikely, and adding -ish makes it moderately so.

clue.text: Amphibian that hurt tip of nose in Telford, for example

indicators.note: the tip of something is its very front end, so only the opening letter is wanted

blocks.note: the cry of someone in pain

explanation.surface: A newt nipped someone on the nose in a Shropshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Telford is a town in Shropshire, England, built after the Second World War as a planned new town.
explanation.definitionFit: A new town is a planned post-war British settlement, and Telford is one example of the type.

clue.text: Rugby player insecure, then over-confident

explanation.surface: A rugby player is nervous at first, then far too cocky.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby union the loose forwards are the flankers and number eight, who play in the back row of the scrum.

clue.text: North American saying to turn around long seat

indicators.note: to turn around is to face the other way, so the letters are read from the end

blocks.note: a motto is a short saying

explanation.surface: An American proverb urges everyone to swivel round on a long bench.
explanation.definitionFit: An ottoman is a low upholstered seat or couch without back or arms, often long enough for several people.

clue.text: Sanctioned audibly in speech

indicators.note: in speech means as the word is spoken, so its sound counts, not its spelling

explanation.surface: Something formally approved by being announced out loud.
explanation.definitionFit: Sanctioned and allowed are both past participles meaning permitted or authorised.

clue.text: Carpeting which may be done on casual Friday?

definitions.text: which may be done on casual Friday

blocks.note: first meaning: a severe telling-off, as when someone is called on the carpet

blocks.clueFragment: which may be done on casual Friday
blocks.note: second meaning: wearing less formal clothes than usual

explanation.surface: A reprimand handed out on the one day the office relaxes its dress code.
explanation.walkthrough: Carpeting looks like floor covering, but here it is the British sense of a severe reprimand. Casual Friday is the end-of-week custom of wearing informal clothes to work.
explanation.definitionFit: A dressing-down is a scolding, and dressing down also means choosing more casual clothes than usual.

clue.text: Article about Lineker ultimately backing female football pundit

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the name is kept
backing means supporting from behind, so this group follows the next piece

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece on Gary Lineker supports a woman pundit on the football show.
explanation.walkthrough: Gary Lineker and Alan Shearer, both former England strikers, were fellow pundits on the BBC's Match of the Day.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Shearer, former England captain, is a well-known television football analyst.

clue.text: Offensive order in the course of row

indicators.note: something happening in the course of another sits within it, so one piece goes inside

blocks.note: a row is a loud din
the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: An insulting command given during a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: Row is the noise sense (rhymes with cow), not a line; OM, the Order of Merit, sits inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Noisome means foul-smelling or disgusting, so it is offensive to the senses.

clue.text: Last bit of fish Paul oddly rejected

indicators.note: throwing out the odd-numbered letters leaves only the second and fourth

blocks.note: a fin is part of a fish

explanation.surface: Paul, being strange, turned down the final morsel of his fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Final and last both describe what comes at the very end of a series.

clue.text: Items in the distance, old British coins

explanation.surface: Objects glimpsed far off turn out to be antique pennies.
explanation.walkthrough: Items in the distance are far things. A farthing was a pre-1961 British coin worth a quarter of an old penny.
explanation.definitionFit: Farthings were small British coins worth a quarter of a penny, withdrawn in 1961.

clue.text: Athletes in Three Peaks Race who come 2nd and 3rd?

blocks.note: first meaning: competitors who literally run up mountains
second meaning: those placed behind the winner

explanation.surface: Fell runners in a mountain race who take silver and bronze.
explanation.walkthrough: The Three Peaks Race is a Yorkshire fell race over three hills, so its runners run up; read together the phrase is the term for those placed behind the winner.
explanation.definitionFit: Runners-up are the competitors who finish just behind the winner, typically second and third.

clue.text: Note women's rent – it's surprisingly put down again

indicators.note: a surprising outcome is not what you expect, so these letters end in an unexpected order

blocks.note: re is a note of the sol-fa scale
W is the abbreviation for women

explanation.surface: A memo about the women's rent says it has unexpectedly been reduced again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put down' looks like reduced, but it means written down; the 's after it is just part of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To rewrite something is to write it out again, so rewritten means set down on paper a second time.

clue.text: Wicket, dreadful error besetting one anxious type

indicators.note: something dreadful is in a terrible state, so the letters are jumbled
to beset is to surround on all sides, so the jumble goes around the next piece

blocks.note: W is the cricket scoring abbreviation for wicket

explanation.surface: A cricketer frets after a terrible mistake costs a wicket.
explanation.definitionFit: A worrier is a person who habitually frets, which makes them an anxious sort.

clue.text: Alternatively, I set an amended crossword at last

indicators.note: amended means altered, so these letters are put into a changed order
at last points to the very end of the word, so only its final letter is used

explanation.surface: A setter admits they finally changed the puzzle, offering another one.
explanation.definitionFit: Instead and alternatively are both adverbs meaning as a substitute or other option.

clue.text: Relative eating first serving of Indian corn, perhaps

indicators.note: eating takes something inside, so one piece goes into the other
the first serving is the opening helping, so only the initial letter is taken

explanation.surface: Grandma tucks into the first helping of an Indian meal with sweetcorn.
explanation.definitionFit: Corn is a cereal crop, an example of grain, as the 'perhaps' signals.

clue.text: Going north abroad, an Argentinian takes in part of Spain

indicators.note: to take in is to contain, so the letters are found running inside the words
in a down entry, going north means travelling upward, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: the letters running across these words

explanation.surface: An Argentinian travelling overseas heads north to visit a Spanish region.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a journey; the run of letters spans the end of abroad and the start of Argentinian.
explanation.definitionFit: Granada is a city and province of Andalusia in southern Spain, home of the Alhambra.

clue.text: What you do here to support sailor is clear

indicators.note: in a down entry, a supporting piece sits underneath, so the sailor goes on top

blocks.note: what a solver does with a crossword

explanation.surface: An instruction to prop up a seaman, which is supposedly obvious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Here' is the crossword in front of you, so what you do is solve it.
explanation.definitionFit: To absolve is to clear someone of blame or guilt, so the two verbs share that sense.

clue.text: Producer of Hairspray under pressure?

blocks.note: surface reading: the impresario behind the stage musical Hairspray, feeling the strain
setter's reading: a pressurised can that dispenses spray for hair

explanation.surface: The backer of the musical Hairspray is feeling stressed.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital H makes Hairspray the Broadway musical; really it is ordinary hairspray, which comes from a can under pressure.
explanation.definitionFit: An aerosol is a pressurised container that releases its contents, such as hairspray, as a fine mist.

clue.text: Animal caught by loop occasionally – this?

definitions.text: Animal caught by loop occasionally – this?

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so every other letter is taken
something caught is held inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: first and third letters of loop

explanation.surface: Is this what's sometimes used to catch an animal with a loop?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: a lasso is a rope loop that sometimes catches animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A lasso is a rope with a running noose thrown to catch cattle or horses.

clue.text: Went past England's opener, run out

indicators.note: an opener comes first, so the opening letter alone is wanted

blocks.note: a licence that has lapsed has run out

explanation.surface: England's opening batsman went past the ball and was run out.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket picture misleads: an opener is the first batsman, but here it just means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Time that has elapsed has gone by, so it went past.

clue.text: Daughter accompanying comedian Joan in clubs

indicators.note: accompanying means going alongside, so the two pieces sit next to each other

explanation.surface: A girl goes along with Joan Rivers on a night out at the clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: Clubs suggests nightspots, but these are golf clubs.
explanation.definitionFit: Drivers are golf clubs used for long shots from the tee.

clue.text: Tolerate high-flying summer visitor

blocks.note: first meaning: to put up with
second meaning: a migratory bird that arrives in Britain for summer

explanation.walkthrough: High-flying summer visitor sounds like a celebrity guest, but it is a bird that migrates to Britain each summer.
explanation.definitionFit: To swallow something is to accept it without protest, and the swallow is a migratory bird that arrives in spring.

clue.text: Bent copper failed to get top spot

indicators.note: something bent is twisted out of shape, so the following letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A corrupt policeman misses out on promotion to the leading position.
explanation.walkthrough: Bent looks like an adjective for the copper (slang for corrupt police officer), but it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Pride of place is the most prominent or honoured position, the top spot.
